Karl Friston

Karl Friston (1959–) has developed the most comprehensive mathematical framework for the brain-as-world-modeler thesis 1, 2, 3. The free energy principle states that any self-organizing system that persists in a changing environment must minimize variational free energy—an information-theoretic quantity that bounds the surprise (surprisal) of sensory observations given the system’s internal generative model. This single imperative subsumes perception (updating the model to reduce prediction error), action (changing sensory input to match predictions), learning (optimizing model parameters), and attention (adjusting the precision of prediction errors). The brain, on this account, is a hierarchical generative model, and everything it does—from saccadic eye movements to abstract reasoning—is variational inference. The mathematical apparatus of the free energy principle, including the role of Markov blankets in defining the boundary between agent and environment, provides the formal backbone of much of this textbook. Andy Clark

Andy Clark (1957–) has been the most prominent philosophical interpreter and champion of the predictive processing framework 4, 5. He argues that the brain is fundamentally a prediction machine: a system that proactively generates top-down expectations about incoming signals and updates itself only when those predictions fail. Perception, on this view, is “controlled hallucination”—an ongoing, largely successful attempt to predict the sensory stream from the inside out. Clark’s earlier work with Chalmers on the extended mind thesis 6 argued that cognitive processes can extend beyond the skull into notebooks, tools, and digital devices, raising the question of whether the world model has a fixed boundary.

Jakob Hohwy

Jakob Hohwy (1974–) has provided the most sustained philosophical analysis of predictive processing as a theory of mind 7. If the brain is a prediction engine locked behind the sensory surfaces—what Hohwy calls the “evidentiary boundary” of the skull—then all it ever has access to are its own prediction errors. The world model is the brain’s best hypothesis about the hidden causes of its sensory states. This leads to an inferential seclusion: the brain never contacts the world directly, only its own best guess about the world—an updated, formally precise rehabilitation of the Kantian predicament.

Thomas Metzinger

Thomas Metzinger (1958–) offers a theory of subjectivity grounded in self-modeling 8. The conscious self is not an entity but a transparent self-model—the phenomenal self-model (PSM)—generated by the brain. “Transparent” means that we do not experience the model as a model; we look through it and experience it as unmediated reality. Consciousness is an “ego tunnel” 9: a low-dimensional, integrated self-world model that the organism cannot see the edges of. This account connects directly to the hierarchical generative model: the self is just another layer of the brain’s world model—the layer that models the modeler.

Evan Thompson

Evan Thompson (1962–) has extended and deepened the enactivist tradition into the era of predictive processing 10, 11. Cognition, he argues, is not a brain process but a relational process involving brain, body, and environment—a view that is continuous with Varela’s autopoietic framework and Merleau-Ponty’s embodied phenomenology. Thompson offers a critical counterpoint to internalist versions of predictive processing: if the world model is understood as an internal neuronal structure, then the embodied, embedded, environmentally coupled character of actual cognition may be lost. The tension between the skull-bound generative model and the world-involving enactive agent is one of the most productive open questions in the field, and it runs through every chapter that follows.

Anil Seth

Anil Seth (1972–) has extended the predictive processing framework inward, from exteroceptive perception to interoception and affect 12, 13. His “beast machine” thesis holds that the most fundamental layer of conscious selfhood arises not from the brain’s model of the external world but from its predictions about the body’s own internal physiological states—visceral, hormonal, and autonomic signals that constitute the felt sense of being alive. Perception, on Seth’s account, is “controlled hallucination” not only of the external scene but of the embodied self that inhabits it. He has also urged a pragmatic reorientation of consciousness science away from Chalmers’s “hard problem” and toward what he calls the “real problem”: explaining, predicting, and experimentally controlling the specific, fine-grained correspondences between neural mechanisms and particular qualities of conscious experience.

Giulio Tononi

Giulio Tononi (1960–) has developed Integrated Information Theory (IIT), the most mathematically ambitious attempt to identify consciousness with a measurable physical quantity 14, 15. IIT proposes that a system is conscious to the extent that it possesses integrated information, denoted Φ\Phi: a measure of how much the system’s current state is simultaneously differentiated (capable of occupying a vast repertoire of distinct states) and integrated (such that the whole generates more information than the sum of its independently considered parts). A system with high Φ\Phi is conscious; one with Φ=0\Phi = 0 is not, regardless of its behavior or functional organization. IIT offers an instructive contrast to the free energy principle: where predictive processing characterizes what the brain does (minimize prediction error through inference), IIT attempts to characterize what a conscious system is (a structure with high integrated information)—and to derive the quality and content of experience from the intrinsic geometry of that structure rather than from its input–output relations.

Lisa Feldman Barrett

Lisa Feldman Barrett (1963–) has extended predictive processing into the domain of affect and emotion with the theory of constructed emotion 16, 17. Against the classical view that emotions are triggered reactions mediated by dedicated neural circuits (a “fear circuit,” a “disgust circuit”), Barrett argues that the brain constructs emotional experiences through the same domain-general, predictive, categorization-based machinery it uses for all perception. Interoceptive signals from the body are inherently ambiguous—a racing heart may signify fear, excitement, or exercise—and the brain resolves this ambiguity by predicting the most probable cause given the current context and the organism’s learned conceptual repertoire. The resulting emotion is a prediction, not a detection. Barrett’s concept of the “body budget” (allostasis) reframes the brain’s deepest function: before it is a perceiver or a thinker, the brain is an organ of metabolic regulation, continuously predicting and managing the body’s energetic needs. Her work demonstrates that the world model is not limited to the external scene; it encompasses the affective and physiological interior, and that the felt quality of experience—whether the world seems threatening, welcoming, or dull—is itself a construction of the generative model, shaped as much by visceral prediction as by sensory input.

Michael Graziano

Michael Graziano (1967–) has proposed Attention Schema Theory (AST), a mechanistic account that treats consciousness as a specific variety of self-modeling 18, 19. Just as the brain constructs a body schema—a simplified internal model of the body’s geometry, posture, and capabilities—it constructs an attention schema: a simplified, schematic model of its own attentional processes. When the brain directs attention to a stimulus, the attention schema represents this process as a mental possession of the stimulus—an internal, subjective experience of it. This schema is what we introspectively report as “awareness.” AST thus reframes consciousness not as a metaphysical mystery but as a modeling problem with a specific computational function: by representing its own attentional states, the brain can monitor, predict, and control where and how it allocates processing resources. The theory also provides a natural account of social cognition—because we model attention in others using the same schema machinery, we readily attribute consciousness to other minds, to animals, and even to animated objects. For the world-modeling framework of this book, Graziano’s contribution is the insight that the model is recursive: the brain models the external world, the body within it, and—crucially—the very process of modeling itself, and it is this last, self-referential layer that generates the felt sense of being a conscious subject.
